highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture [Con76, p. 46] says: if $ab=cd$ for omnific integers, then $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$, $d=fh$ for some omnific integers $e,f,g,h$. In an integral domain this is the same as saying that every element is primal. Conway normal form identifies the omnific integers with a ring of generalised power series, $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$. The guide proves that every element of this ring is primal. It proves the same for $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ under conditions on $G$ that include (A1)--(A3) of [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]. There are four ideas.

Germs. Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and $G$ a Cauchy-complete ordered abelian group. Let $J$ be the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class of $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ modulo $J$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. Germs obey the convolution formula, which for $G=\mathbb R$ is [Ber00, Lem. 7.5]. The Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closed support drops along germs just below $0$.

Transcendence. Germs that are new at a given rank are transcendental over the germs already present. Adjoining them one at a time shows that $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ is a polynomial ring over $K$. So $J$ is prime; for $G=\mathbb R$ this is [Ber00, Cor. 9.8]. The same method shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over the series with finite support. So $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain.

Reduction along Archimedean classes. Grouping exponents along a convex subgroup gives a $D+M$ construction. Primality then reduces to two smaller problems. At the leading Archimedean class the exponents become real, and the GCD theorem applies. At a limit of classes, primality of germs and an induction on the classes finish the proof.

Surreal exponents. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets gives the cofinality and completeness that the reduction needs. Conway normal form takes the result back to the omnific integers.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
This chapter proves the facts about germs that the next chapter needs. If $G$ is Cauchy complete, germs obey the convolution formula, which carries the main idea of the chapter. The germs of $b^{|\gamma}$ are the germs of $b$, shifted by $\gamma$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is nonzero exactly when $\gamma$ is in the closure of the support. It is a constant exactly when the germs just below $\gamma$ vanish.

Inductions use the Cantor--Bendixson value of $0$ in the closed support. It depends only on the germ. If the germ is not a constant, the value drops along the germs just below $0$.
phases.setting: $K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity. For $b\in K((G^{\le0}))$ and $\gamma\in G$, $b_{|\gamma}$ is the truncation of $b$ at $\gamma$, the part of $b$ with exponents at most $\gamma$, and $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ is the translated truncation, again an element of $K((G^{\le0}))$. $J$ is the ideal of series whose support is bounded away from $0$, $[b]$ is the class of $b$ in $K((G^{\le0}))/J$, and $K$ is identified with its image there. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is $[b^{|\gamma}]$, and $V_{\mathrm{CB}}(b)$ is the Cantor--Bendixson value of $b$.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
The key statement is the transcendence lemma: if $S\subseteq[A_S]$ is a domain and $X$ has its germs below $0$ in $S$ but $x=[X]\notin S$, then $x$ is transcendental over $S$. Its proof takes a relation of least degree and applies the germ maps to it. Two lemmas prepare it: $x$ satisfies no linear relation over $S$, and germs that are proportional near $0$ are proportional by a constant.

Adjoining such germs one at a time shows that $Q$ is a polynomial ring over $K$ when $G$ is Cauchy complete. So $J$ is prime. The same holds for series with support of cardinality less than $\kappa$.

For real exponents, a series has only constant germs exactly when its support is finite. The same method then shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support. That subring is a GCD domain [LM24, Fact 2.5.2]. By Gauss's lemma, $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain too.
phases.setting:
$K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity. Write $A=K((G^{\le0}))$ and $Q=A/J$. The germs of $b\in A$ are the classes $[b^{|\xi}]$, $\xi\in G$. For $a=[b]\in Q$ put $\operatorname{rk}(a)=V_{\mathrm{CB}}(b)$, which depends only on $a$. For a $K$-subalgebra $S\subseteq Q$, $A_S$ is the set of series all of whose germs lie in $S$, and $S\subseteq[A_S]$ means that every element of $S$ is $[b]$ for some $b\in A_S$. A $K$-subalgebra $R\subseteq A$ is closed under the truncations $b\mapsto b_{|\eta}$ if $b_{|\eta}\in R$ for all $b\in R$ and $\eta\in G$. $K(G^{\le0})$ is the subring of series with finite support.

Hypothesis (H): $G$ is Cauchy complete, $S\subseteq Q$ is a $K$-subalgebra with $S\subseteq[A_S]$, $X\in A$ satisfies $[X^{|\xi}]\in S$ for all $\xi<0$, and $x=[X]$.

phases.title: Reduction along Archimedean classes
phases.description:
This chapter proves that every element of $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal under conditions on $G$. Regrouping exponents along a convex subgroup $C$ turns $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ into a $D+M$ construction with $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. So $x$ is primal if its regrouping $\hat x$ and its restriction $x_{|C}$ are primal; this is the statement that carries the reduction.

The proof is an induction on the Archimedean classes met by the support. If there are finitely many, take $C$ below the leading class; the regrouped series has real exponents, so it is primal by the GCD theorem. If there are infinitely many, take $C$ below a limit of classes. Then the regrouped series is primal because its germ is primal, by the polynomial presentation of the ring of germs, and because restrictions to Archimedean balls split off factors with fewer classes.

The chapter ends with a converse: the refinement property forces $R$ to be the fraction field of $Z$.
phases.setting:
$G$ is an ordered abelian group, $R$ a field, $Z\subseteq R$ a subring, and $\kappa>\aleph_0$ a cardinal. $R((G))_\kappa$ is the field of series whose support has cardinality less than $\kappa$, and $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ its subring of series with nonpositive support and constant coefficient in $Z$. An element meets the Archimedean classes of the exponents in its support. For a convex subgroup $C$, $x_{|C}$ is the restriction of $x$ to $C$. For a nonzero Archimedean class $\sigma$, $G_{\prec\sigma}$ and $G_{\preceq\sigma}$ are the convex subgroups of elements of class smaller than $\sigma$, respectively at most $\sigma$, in magnitude, and $H_\sigma$ is a fixed complement of $G_{\prec\sigma}$ in $G_{\preceq\sigma}$. For a set $T$ of nonzero classes, $H_T=\bigcap_{\sigma\in T}G_{\preceq\sigma}$.

For a convex subgroup $C$ that is a subspace for the scalars in use, put $\Gamma=G/C$, $L=R((C))_\kappa$ and $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. Regrouping exponents along a complement of $C$ sends $x$ to $\hat x\in L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$, with constant coefficient $x_{|C}$; it identifies $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ with $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$.

Conditions [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]: (A1)$_\sigma$: $H_\sigma\simeq\mathbb R$ as ordered groups. (A2)$_\sigma$: $\operatorname{cf}(G_{\prec\sigma})\ge\kappa$, or $G_{\prec\sigma}=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (A3): $Z$ is pre-Schreier. Further conditions, for a set $T$ of nonzero classes: (B1)$_T$: $\operatorname{cf}(H_T)\ge\kappa$, or $H_T=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (B2)$_T$: $G/H_T$ is Cauchy complete for its order topology and group uniformity.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
This chapter checks the conditions of the general theorem for surreal exponents. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets carries the argument.

Each Archimedean complement in $\mathbf{No}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Conway's construction gives the needed cofinalities. It also fills small cuts, and a cut criterion turns this into Cauchy completeness of the quotients of $\mathbf{No}$.

So every element of $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal. Conway normal form identifies this ring with the omnific integers. Hence the omnific integers have the refinement property, and every irreducible omnific integer is prime.
phases.setting: $\mathbf{No}$ is the field of surreal numbers of a fixed universe $u$, $\kappa_u$ the cardinal of that universe, and $\mathbf{Oz}\subseteq\mathbf{No}$ the ring of omnific integers. Archimedean classes, $\mathbf{No}_{\prec\sigma}$, $\mathbf{No}_{\preceq\sigma}$ and $H_T$ are as in the previous chapter, with $G=\mathbf{No}$.
